desc:
The array sides holds non-negative stick lengths. Count the triples of positions i < j < k such that the three lengths can be the sides of a triangle with positive area, that is, each length is strictly smaller than the sum of the other two.

sides = [2, 2, 3, 4]
valid triples: (2,2,3), (2,3,4), (2,3,4)
result = 3

Sticks of length 0 never take part in a valid triangle. Equal lengths at different positions count as different sticks.
hints: For three lengths a ≤ b ≤ c, which of the three triangle inequalities is the only one that can fail?
Only a + b > c matters (the others hold automatically for sorted values). Sort the array and fix the longest side c by index.
With c = s[k] fixed, use i = 0 and j = k - 1. If s[i] + s[j] > s[k], all of s[i..j-1] pair with s[j]: add j - i and decrement j. Otherwise increment i.
editorial: Sort the lengths. For sorted values a ≤ b ≤ c, the inequalities a + c > b and b + c > a are automatic when the lengths are positive, so the triple is valid exactly when a + b > c. With zeros, a = 0 gives b > c, which contradicts b ≤ c, so zero sticks are rejected by the same test.

Fix the longest side at sorted index k and search the prefix 0..k-1 for pairs (i, j) with s[i] + s[j] > s[k]. Start with i = 0, j = k - 1. If s[i] + s[j] > s[k], then every index between i and j - 1 also works with j (they are at least as big as s[i]), which adds j - i pairs; then j is done. If the sum is not big enough, i can never help with a partner at most s[j], so advance i.
This is O(n²) in total (a linear sweep for each of the n choices of k) plus the sort.
